extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for reviewers evaluating submissions to CVPR 2023, covering ethics, conflicts of interest, how to write reviews, handling rebuttals/supplementary material, and technical evaluation standards. Intended to direct reviewers' behavior and the content/quality of their reviews for this conference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical soundness and contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Each paper that is accepted should be technically sound and make a contribution to the field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for what is good or stimulating in the paper, and what knowledge advancement it has made. Be specific about the contribution and technical correctness before recommending acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh novelty and impact alongside reported performance
rubrics_metrics.description: We recommend that you embrace novel, brave concepts, even if they have not been tested on many datasets. The fact that a proposed method does not exceed the state-of-the-art accuracy on an existing benchmark dataset is not grounds for rejection by itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Weigh both the novelty and potential impact of the work alongside reported performance. Do not reject solely because the method does not beat SOTA on a benchmark; consider potential and innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minor flaws should not justify rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Minor flaws that can be easily corrected should not be a reason to reject a paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify and describe minor issues and suggest corrections rather than using them as the primary reason for rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific and detailed in reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Your discussion, more than your score, will help the authors, fellow reviewers, and Area Chairs understand the basis for your recommendation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include specific feedback on ways the authors can improve their papers. Short reviews are unhelpful; avoid single-sentence bullets — explain reasoning and provide actionable suggestions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check assignments for conflicts and comfort to review
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as you get your reviewing assignment, please go through all the papers to make sure that (a) you have no obvious conflict of interest and (b) you feel comfortable reviewing the paper assigned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If issues arise about conflict or comfort, contact the Area Chair immediately as instructed. Do not proceed to write a review if you believe a conflict exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and apply official author/policy guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Please read the Author Guidelines carefully to familiarize yourself with all official policies the authors are expected to follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you suspect a paper violates a policy, contact the Chairs. In the meantime, proceed to review the paper assuming no violation has taken place.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect anonymity in the review process
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should not take active steps to discover the identity of the authors, and make all efforts to keep their own identity invisible to the authors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to find author identities by web searching. If you happen to know or suspect authors (e.g., via arXiv), you may still review as long as you can be impartial. Do not reveal your identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect confidentiality of ideas and materials
rubrics_metrics.description: As a reviewer you have the responsibility to protect the confidentiality of the ideas represented in the papers you review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not show the paper, results, videos/images, code, or supplementary material to non-reviewers. Do not use ideas/code from papers you review to develop your own work. After the process, destroy copies of papers/supplementary material and erase any implementations/results produced while evaluating the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflicts of interest: general prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important for you to avoid any conflict of interest. There should be absolutely no question about the impartiality of any review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a review would create a possible conflict of interest, return the paper and do not submit a review. Contact the Area Chair to arrange reassignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid conflicts of interest: examples of COI
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicts of interest include (but are not limited to): working at the same institution as an author; being directly involved in the work; suspected perceptual conflicts; recent collaborations (about past three years); advisor/advisee relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use judgment for collaboration definition (e.g., co-authored papers or proposals). Consider advisor/advisee status carefully — historically treated as a strong conflict, especially recent ones. If in doubt, contact the AC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be professional and constructive in tone
rubrics_metrics.description: Belittling or sarcastic comments have no place in the reviewing process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write courteous, informative, incisive, and helpful reviews. Word criticisms constructively. Avoid attacking the authors; focus on the paper. Aim to write a review you would be proud to sign if it were not anonymous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take time to form your review
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideally, you should read a paper and then think about it over the course of several days before you write your review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid rushed, short reviews. Put effort into thoughtful, detailed feedback rather than quick judgments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be specific when suggesting writing improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Be specific when you suggest that the writing needs to be improved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point to particular sections that are unclear and give concrete suggestions for how to clarify them rather than vague comments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support claims about novelty with references
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims in a review that the submitted work 'has been done before' MUST be backed up with specific references and an explanation of how closely they are related.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claiming lack of novelty, provide citations and explain differences. For positive reviews, explicitly summarize the most interesting novel aspects in the Strengths section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not reject solely for missing citations or arXiv comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not reject papers solely because they are missing citations or comparisons to prior work that has only been published without review (e.g., arXiv or technical reports).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors are not required to thoroughly compare with recent arXiv reports. Failing to cite or beat an arXiv paper should not by itself be grounds for rejection. If you suspect plagiarism, raise it with Program Chairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not ask authors to cite multiple of your own papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not give away your identity by asking the authors to cite several of your own papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid self-promotional citation requests; these can reveal reviewer identity and are unethical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope judgments: explain and suggest alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: If you think the paper is out of scope for CVPR's subject areas, clearly explain why in the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggest other publication possibilities (journals, conferences, workshops) that would be a better match. Nonetheless, keep an open mind unless the mismatch is extreme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use third-person, avoid confrontational phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid referring to the authors in the second person ('you'). It is best to avoid the term 'the authors' as well; instead, use the third person ('the paper').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second-person or direct addressing can be perceived as confrontational. Use neutral wording focused on the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be generous with improvement suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Be generous about giving the authors new ideas for how they can improve their work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggest technical tools, datasets, application areas, or generalizations that could increase impact. Provide constructive, actionable guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplementary material: consult only as needed; adhere to rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The supplementary material is intended to provide details of derivations and results that do not fit within the paper format or space limit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult supplementary material only if helpful to understand the paper. Per Author Guidelines, supplementary material MAY NOT include results obtained with an improved version of the method or updated/corrected submission PDFs. If you find violations, contact the Area Chair.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal requests should avoid asking for substantial new experiments
rubrics_metrics.description: In your review, you may request clarifications or additional illustrations in the rebuttal. Reviewers should not request substantial additional experiments for the rebuttal, or penalize for lack of additional experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Substantial' refers to what would be needed in a major revision. Rebuttals may include figures or comparison tables; do not penalize for authors supplying extra results, but you may choose to ignore them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media posts about submissions are not automatically violations
rubrics_metrics.description: If a social media post shared information on a CVPR submission without the authors being involved, that does not, by itself, signal a violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A violation occurs only when authors are proactively sharing. If you suspect author involvement, raise it with Chairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling withdrawn datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice to use a withdrawn dataset, while not in itself grounds for rejection, should invite very close scrutiny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flag such cases for AC/PC consideration. Consider whether authors explain why they used it, whether that explanation is compelling, and whether alternatives exist. If the paper could be accepted without experiments on the withdrawn dataset, advise removing those experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers cannot require experiments on withdrawn datasets
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a violation of policy for a reviewer or Area Chair to require comparison on a dataset that has been withdrawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not ask authors to evaluate on a withdrawn dataset; instead evaluate on other merits or suggest alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluating dataset-as-contribution claims
rubrics_metrics.description: If a paper submission is claiming a dataset as one of its contributions, there should be a reasonable expectation that the dataset will be made publicly available upon publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use judgment: private or restricted datasets are not required and are not grounds for rejection, but they cannot be claimed as contributions in their own right. Evaluate the paper on other technical merits if dataset won't be public.

rubrics_metrics.name: No fixed quota for acceptance/rejection per reviewer
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no minimum number of papers a reviewer should accept or reject.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate each paper on its own. If you feel most assigned papers have value, accept them; if many are poor, provide clear and very specific comments for each. Do NOT assume your stack should mirror the conference acceptance rate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling suspected plagiarism or prior short publications
rubrics_metrics.description: If a reviewer identifies a prior short paper (e.g., ICASSP/ICASSP four-page) with substantial overlap, that prior short paper is not automatically considered a 'previous publication' under dual submission policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether the CVPR submission offers enough additional value. If it does not add enough value, it may be rejected on substantive grounds. If there is a possibility of plagiarism (different authors), contact the Area Chair to investigate.
